Zachary's Law

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
-In the fight between money and medicine, a little boy’s life is the line they’re willing to cross.

Unique Selling Point:
Zachary’s Law: STORY PITCH
A David vs Goliath story of when a Medical Aid Defies the Law
ONE LINE SUMMARY: A mother won in court. Twice. But her medical aid still refuses to pay for her child’s rare disease. Now, a judge has said: obey — or go to jail to the medical aid.
It started as one mother’s desperate fight to save her son.
Now, it could change how medical aids treat every South African patient.
A 5-year-old boy, Zachary De Wet, has Hunter Syndrome (MPS II) — a rare genetic condition that slowly attacks the body and the brain. There’s only one treatment that can slow it down: Elaprase, an enzyme-replacement drug.
Yet, his family’s medical aid — Medihelp — refused to pay.
Initially, Medihelp argued in court that Elaprase was not a Prescribed Minimum Benefit (PMB).
But in 2022, a judge rejected that argument — ruling that not only is the condition a PMB, but that the standard for determining treatment is simple: “What does the state do?”
And in this case, the state provides Elaprase. They then argued that while the state gives the drug, it’s only done through a “compassionate programme” — so they weren’t obliged to fund it.
That single interpretation has now exploded into one of the biggest legal fights in South African healthcare.
THE STORY:
Zachary’s mother, Michaney De Wet, turned to attorney Megan Harrington-Johnson — a name Carte Blanche audiences will recognise. We previously told Megan’s own story, when she fought for her daughter’s future after a childhood cancer diagnosis — using cutting-edge science to preserve her little girl’s chance of having children one day.
Now, she’s on the other side of the table — fighting for another family, against a medical aid giant.
Her firm took the case pro bono in 2021, arguing that because the state provides Elaprase, it must also be covered by private medical aids under the law governing PMBs.
Different layers: The First Win (2022)
Judge Millar rules in favour of the De Wets:
• Hunter Syndrome (MPS II) is a PMB condition.
• Elaprase is the standard public-sector treatment — so Medihelp must pay for it.
• The ruling sets a powerful precedent for rare-disease coverage.
Despite this, Medihelp refused to pay, and backed by an army of advocates representing other medical schemes, they appealed.
According to Kelly du Plessis of Rare Diseases South Africa, this fight went far beyond a single family’s struggle.
“This wasn’t just one fund defending itself — it was the entire medical-aid industry protecting its profit model.”
Layer 2: The Showdown (2025)
Last week, Judge Swanepoel handed down a scathing judgment.
He upheld the earlier decision and went further — finding Medihelp in contempt of court for ignoring Judge Millar’s order.
He wrote that Medihelp’s conduct was “cynical, aggressive, and mala fide” — and warned that if they don’t pay, the Principal Officer could be imprisoned.
It’s one of the most blistering rebukes of a medical aid ever seen in South Africa.
Megan HJ: Two judges. Two rulings. One medical aid defying them both.
CHARACTERS:
• Zachary (5) — bright, funny, and brave. He still receives his life-saving treatment through donations, but his future depends on this ruling being enforced.
• Michaney De Wet — a mother who’s spent years fighting bureaucracy while trying to keep her son alive.
• Megan Harrington-Johnson — lawyer, mother, and rare-disease advocate. Her personal story gives this case an extraordinary emotional echo.
• Rare Diseases South Africa (Kelly du Plessis) — the NGO that’s stepped in where medical aids have failed, supporting families like Zachary’s across the country.
EXTRA INFORMATION:
Carte Blanche first explored this issue in 2022 — exposing how families with rare diseases were being denied essential, life-sustaining treatments.
This case takes that story a decisive step further. At its core, it asks a fundamental question of South African healthcare law: must medical aids meet the same standard of care provided by the state? Since that earlier report, medical aids have continued to delay or deny enzyme replacement therapies (ERTs) — even when medical and legal evidence shows these treatments must be fully funded. Now, for the first time, a medical aid has been found in contempt of court for refusing to provide care-related treatment. The ruling sets a powerful new precedent: PMB conditions can’t be defined by whether the state pays for treatment, but by whether that treatment is available within the state system — even if supplied through a compassionate or donor programme.
We’ll, of course, request an interview with Medihelp — though it’s unlikely they’ll agree. In that case, we can head to their head offices in Brooklyn, Pretoria, and give viewers some context about who they are. Medihelp has been operating since 1905 and today serves more than 200,000 members. In 2023, the scheme reported R2.39 billion in assets and paid out R3.3 billion in claims. As Principal Officer, Varsha Vala is the public face of Medihelp’s leadership — and in this story, she’s the person whose accountability will come under scrutiny if the scheme continues to defy two court orders.
I believe this story will hold strong until January, as Medihelp is expected to seek leave to appeal to the Constitutional Court. That means the legal battle — and public interest — will remain active. Even if the court process takes time, the core issue of accountability won’t date: a major medical aid defying two High Court orders and facing possible contempt proceedings is a story that will stay relevant and develop further in the months ahead.

Summary:
Zachary’s Law -In the fight between money and medicine, a little boy’s life is the line they’re willing to cross.________________________________________
Opening Act
[OPENING – VISUAL SEQUENCE]
Raining, water dripping, and it dissolves into a drip bag filling – an infusion. The drip line is prepared for infusion by Zach’s parents…
See Zachary getting the infusion. Govan watches.
(Govan VO) This tiny vial carries a price tag of R3 million a year, and it’s the treatment that keeps Zach alive. And although he’s able to get it today… it’s because it’s being donated, not because his medical aid is paying.
(Govan link) Imagine hearing your child needs life-saving treatment — and then your medical aid turns you away. What would you do? For Jacques and Michaney de Wet, the answer was simple: you fight.
(Govan VO) Zachary is five years old. He has a rare genetic condition called Hunter Syndrome — or MPS II — that slowly attacks the body and brain. There’s only one treatment that can slow the disease down: Elaprase. Each vial costs thousands of rand, and he needs it every week.
(Govan Link) To understand this case, we need to talk about something called a Prescribed Minimum Benefit — or a PMB. It’s the law that protects every medical-aid member in South Africa. And for families like Zachary’s, it can be the difference between life and death.
(Govan VO) PMBs are the treatments that medical aids must pay for — in full — no matter which plan you’re on, or how much the treatment costs. The law says the standard of care is what the state provides. So if a government hospital offers a particular treatment for a PMB condition, every medical aid has to match it.
Link: In Zachary’s case, the state treats Hunter Syndrome with a drug called Elaprase. That means Elaprase is the legal minimum standard of care. But despite this Medihelp – the families’ medical aid - still refuses to pay.
ACT 1 ends…
RECAP OF previous story:
VO: In 2022, we first met Jacques and Michaney de Wet, and their toddler Zachary.
Michaney: “When he learns something new, you’re almost… holding your breath. Because you don’t know how long he’ll be able to keep it.”
VO: He’s just been newly diagnosed, and they were already facing Medihelp’s refusal to pay.
Jacques: “If his heart deteriorates… if he loses his ability to walk or talk… there’s nothing we can do. That’s why we can’t afford to wait.”
VO: And that’s why our story ended with them going to court.
LINK outside court: Today, that same family stands at the centre of a showdown with three court orders, a contempt ruling, and the possibility of a medical-aid executive going to jail — all because a five-year-old boy needs treatment the law says he must receive.
Fade to black…
Visuals: Footage of Zachary laughing at home, playing with toy cars, his parents preparing his medication day.
Visuals: Cut to Michaney and Jacques interview – intimate home setting.
(Michaney/Jacques) When Medihelp refused to pay, we had no choice. His doctors said without Elaprase, he wouldn’t survive. So we took them to court.
TIMELINE DEVICE:
[Govan VO) [COURT VISUALS / DOCUMENT GRAPHICS] In 2022, Judge Anthony Millar ruled in the family’s favour — finding that Hunter Syndrome is a Prescribed Minimum Benefit, or PMB, and that Elaprase is standard treatment, because it’s provided in public hospitals.
Megan Harrington-Johnson and her firm’s team took the case on pro bono, Medihelp was ordered to pay within 30 days.
(MEGAN HJ) That judgment was clear — the law says medical aids must fund PMB conditions in full. But Medihelp chose to fight instead of pay. But also Millar noted, that the Medihelp conceded it was a PMB.
Read it with Megan…
GOVAN VO: Medihelp’s argument? The family hadn’t filled out the right paperwork. The billing codes were wrong — basically, ‘computer says no.’
You’d think the battle ended there right? But instead, Medihelp would just stall and appeal for the next three years – and refuse to comply with the order the pay.
GOVAN (VO): But what about Zachary in the meantime? His treatment continued thanks to donations and the pharmaceutical company supplying Elaprase while the legal battle drags on.
MICHANEY (to camera): “It’s donated. Every vial. That’s the only reason he’s still alive.”
[TRANSITION – CHILD PLAYING / MUSIC SWELL]
Fade to black. Title card: “ACT 2 – The Bigger Battle”
WHO ARE MEDIHELP?
VO: Medihelp is one of South Africa’s big six open medical schemes — more than 200,000 members, over 120 years old, and entirely non-profit. In 2023 alone, it held more than R2.3 billion in assets and paid out over R3.3 billion in claims. At its helm is Principal Officer Varsha Vala, the person legally responsible for ensuring Medihelp complies with the Medical Schemes Act and with court orders.
LINK: So this isn’t an anonymous bureaucracy. It’s one of the country’s major medical aids — and a leader who could personally face the consequences if the scheme continues to defy the law.

________________________________________
ACT 2 – THE PRECEDENT THAT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING
VO: Timeline: After the 2022 case, Medihelp appealed, and went to the Council for Medical Schemes, while initially they ruled in favour of Medihelp that decision was overturned – and importantly Elaprase was again deemed a PMB.
Megan: Medihelp wants to adhere to the first decision, and is trying to ignore all the other decisions that are not in their favour – which is everything.
VO: But this decision was again appealed by both sides.
Megan: They said that despite it being a PMB, Medihelp didn’t have to pay because weren’t solvent.
GOVAN LINK : This is Medihelp’s strongest defence, they say they legally cannot pay. The scheme told the medical regulator that its solvency ratio has dropped below the required 25 percent — and that funding Elaprase would breach solvency laws and threaten the financial stability of the entire scheme. But the courts have been clear on this: solvency is not an excuse to refuse a Prescribed Minimum Benefit. Judges have rejected this argument every time it’s been raised, saying solvency rules exist to protect members, not to deny them life-saving treatment.
While that appeal process is underway, Megan’s team again took Medihelp to court, which only happened in November last year (THIS WILL AIR IN JAN).
Megan: This was to make them comply with a court order to pay.
VO: In short the court agreed, Medihelp must pay pending the CMS appeal process. However, Judge Swanepoel was scathing.
[COURT GRAPHIC – PULL QUOTES]
“I have no doubt the applicant is in contempt of the order of Millar J.” – Judge Swanepoel, 2025
VO: But went further calling them cynical and their behaviour bad-faith conduct.
“I have no doubt that the applicant has taken the view that it will not fund treatment… and that its conduct is mala fide.”
“In my view the applicant’s conduct is deserving of punishment.”
“The applicant’s explanation for not paying… does not hold water… it is untenable and should be rejected.”
“The applicant has deliberately chosen not to abide by the order…”
SEE GOVAN READING link: If Medihelp does not purge its contempt, the court may issue a writ directing the commanding officer of Brooklyn Police Station to immediately arrest the Principal Officer of Medihelp and commit him/her to prison until the contempt is purged.
That’s a legal first! Principal Officer Varsha Vala could go to jail if they don’t comply.
[VO – GRAPHICS + INTERVIEW]
ACT 3:
VO: For families fighting rare diseases, there is one person they turn to when the system shuts its doors. Kelly du Plessis has walked this road herself as we’ve shown in our previous story— as a mother and as an advocate — she knows better than anyone what happens when medical aids refuse to pay.
KELLY DU PLESSIS (Rare Diseases South Africa): “Medihelp isn’t just fighting one family — it’s defending an entire industry model. Because if this judgment stands, every medical scheme in South Africa will have to match the state’s standard of care.”
GOVAN LINK: “If you read between the lines of Medihelp’s filings — and listen to what’s said quietly — a clearer picture emerges. This fight isn’t really about one child, or one drug. It’s about precedent. If Medihelp pays for Elaprase as Prescribed Minimum Benefit treatment, then every medical aid in South Africa may have to fund these rare-disease therapies in full — therapies that can cost millions a year. And that’s the line the industry doesn’t want to cross. Judge Swanepoel makes the point bluntly in his ruling: Medihelp isn’t fighting the law — they’re fighting the consequences of following it. In other words, they’re fighting precedent… not the child who needs the treatment.”
VO: She says this judgement is so important to hold medical aids accountable.
KELLY DU PLESSIS: Medical aids are now delaying or denying enzyme replacement therapies, even where there’s overwhelming proof they must pay. This is the first time a medical aid’s been held in contempt for refusing care — and it confirms PMB conditions must be judged by availability in the state sector, not whether the state pays.”
GOVAN VO: Some viewers may wonder why Zachary simply go to a government hospital?
[Govan Link: But as his parents explain, that door simply isn’t open. At Charlotte Maxeke, the entire annual budget for paediatric rare-disease treatment is about six million rand — and Zachary’s therapy alone costs half of that. The public system works on a first-come-first-served basis, and once a child starts lifelong therapy, that slot is gone for years. And legally, the state cannot fund treatment for a child already on medical aid. That’s exactly why PMB laws exist — to stop medical aids from pushing complex, expensive patients onto an already overstretched public system. So for Zachary, there is no state alternative. His medical aid is the one legally required to pay, and that’s why this fight matters.]
Jacques: Budget for paediatric rare diseases at Charlotte Maxeke = ±R6 million a year. Zach’s treatment alone costs R3 million. Only one or two patients can be treated at a time. The PMB law exists to prevent private medical aids from dumping patients onto the state.
GOVAN LINK In short, the state can’t take him. The law says his medical aid must.
VO: But Medihelp has made it clear — it will appeal all the way to the Constitutional Court, even if that takes years. Kelly believes it may be cheaper to keep fighting than to pay.
[TRANSITION – COURT GRAPHICS / DOCUMENT SCAN]
Paragraph 42: “Financial hardship cannot justify defying a court order.”
GOVAN LINK (outside Medihelp in Pretoria): “Medihelp has been around since 1905 — one of South Africa’s oldest medical aids, serving more than 200,000 members. We asked them for an interview. They declined. In a written response, Medihelp said it respects the legal process and intends to pursue all available appeals.”
(GOVAN VO) Medihelp denies that it has acted unlawfully. The scheme says it believed the 2022 court order no longer applied after the medical regulator initially ruled that Elaprase was not part of the prescribed minimum benefits. Medihelp maintains it acted in good faith.
GOVAN LINK 3: Medihelp has long argued that Elaprase can’t be considered Prescribed Minimum Benefit treatment because the state doesn’t fund it — even though it’s provided in several government hospitals through donor and compassionate-access programmes. Their position has been simple: if the state doesn’t pay for it, neither should they. But that argument has now been rejected at every level — by the CMS Appeal Committee and by both High Court judges. The law looks at whether the treatment is available in the public sector, not who pays for it. And in Zachary’s case, the state does use Elaprase. Which means medically and legally, it is PMB care.
HAPPIER ENDING – THE MEDS ARE WORKING! YAY!
GOVAN VO: Behind the legal arguments and billion-rand precedents is a little boy whose treatment is working. Doctors say Zachary met every entry criterion and has responded exceptionally well — his disease has stabilised.
MICHANEY (tearful): “It’s easy to forget there’s a child in all of this. Every court date, every delay — that’s time he doesn’t have.”
Cut to Megan HJ: “This isn’t about one case. It’s about whether medical aids think they can outspend the law. And it’s about whether we, as a country, will let them.”
[CLOSING SCENE]
Soft visuals: Zachary plays with his dad; laughter echoes.
GOVAN LINK (closing): “In the end, it’s easy to talk about billions, percentages, and legal precedent — but it all comes down to one small life. And sometimes, the majority doesn’t outweigh the one.”
Fade out.

Teasers:
One: One family. One child. And a medical aid that would rather fight in court than pay to save a life.”
“It’s easy to forget the numbers — until you remember they belong to a five-year-old boy.”
“In the battle over policy, codes, and court orders, it’s easy to lose sight of the truth: a child is running out of time.”
“This isn’t a claims dispute — it’s a fight for a child’s life.”

Zachary’s Law
(Michenay) Zach’s always just been Zach. He’s not the most patient of people, but he's very quick to just love.
(Govan VO) Zach looks like any energetic six-year-old.
(Jacques) Anything that is exaggerated, he loves loud noises, trucks and dinosaurs!
(Govan VO) But then you learn that his body is fighting an incurable rare disease.
(Govan VO) These weekly infusions of a drug called Elaprase keep Zach’s genetic condition — Hunter Syndrome — under control. Without treatment, it damages the body and brain. It's fatal.
But the drug is costly - around R3 million a year - and Zach is receiving it only because it’s being donated — not because his medical aid is paying.
(Govan Link) Imagine hearing your child needs life-saving treatment — and then your medical aid turns you away. What would you do? For Jacques and Michaney de Wet, the answer was simple: you fight.
(Govan VO) That fight has the medical aid industry watching closely. At stake is what a Prescribed Minimum Benefit or PMB— the care medical aids are legally required to fund — actually covers.
(Govan Link) At the heart of this case is a single question: does the law require medical aids to pay for Elaprase — or not? Everyone agrees Hunter Syndrome is a Prescribed Minimum Benefit condition. The dispute is whether funding Elaprase is a legal obligation — or a matter of choice.
(Govan VO) We first met Jacques, Michenay and little Zach de Wet in 2022 when Medihelp first told the family it would not fund Elaprase.
Based in Pretoria, Medihelp is one of the largest non-profit medical aid schemes - with 190,000 members.
The de Wets decided to take the Goliath to court. (Recap over)
(Govan link) Today, three years later, they stand at the centre of a legal showdown involving High Court judgments, the medical regulator, and the possibility of a medical-aid executive going to jail.
(Jacques) Before we went to the High Court, I remember I just spent about half an hour grieving his death, and he was still there.
(Govan) Oh no!
(Jacques) I had to come to terms with the fact that, soon, he might not be with us.
(Govan VO) The family is represented pro bono by a Fourways-based legal team led by attorney Megan Harrington-Johnson.
(Megan) My heart went out to them, being in the situation where you have a critically ill child, and you are now worrying about having to pay for their treatment.
(Govan VO) This complex case has played out in two arenas: the courts, and the medical-aid regulator - the CMS or Council for Medical Schemes. (graphic timeline) In August 2022, High Court Judge Anthony Millar ruled in the family’s favour.
(Megan) What Judge Millar found was that pending the outcome of the dispute in the CMS, so the Council for Medical Schemes, all treatments and associated costs for Zachary's condition, which he confirmed is a PMB condition, must be paid for.
(Govan VO) Medihelp later sought leave to appeal this ruling, but meanwhile began to pay for Elaprase. Zach responded well.
(Michenay) So within about three or four months, we very clearly had that shift from him being sick every six weeks to not having that at all.
(Govan VO) Millar’s order only applied until the CMS process was complete. The family’s complaint about Medihelp’s refusal to pay was heard in December 2022.
(Megan) There is a dispute as to what the standard of care he should be receiving is, because whilst he has to have all of his treatment paid for, it's defined in very broad terms in the Medical Schemes Act. So, it says that he should have medical management paid for, and there's a dispute as to what constitutes medical management.
(Govan VO) Medihelp argues that it’s not obliged to pay for Elaprase - only for broader medical management like hospitalisation. The CMS initially agreed.
(Megan) They said that Judge Miller's order fell away. Unfortunately, the medical aid stopped paying for his treatment.
(Govan VO) Medihelp reasoned that Millar’s order was meant to secure immediate access to Elaprase when Zach had none – and once it was donated, the basis for that order fell away.


(Jacques) That was a shock, because we'd just gone into the rhythm of how life was supposed to be. And now his life saving drug is ripped away from you. (pause)
(Megan) So a third party funder has stepped in to donate the Elaprase to him until such time as the CMS complaint is finalised.
(Govan VO) After appealing the initial CMS finding, the family won the appeal in June 2025: The ruling said Elaprase should be funded. But with a caveat for Medihelp.
(Megan) So the last decision of the CMS strangely found that whilst Zachary's condition should be a PMB entitlement, they were excused from paying because their solvency ratio fell below the threshold of 25%.
(Govan VO) In other words, Medihelp didn't have enough money in its fund to pay for this treatment - at least according to the CMS.
(Govan) But isn't the solvency ratio meant to protect the members, not the medical aides?
(Megan) Yes, correct.
(Govan link) We asked medihelp for an on-camera interview but they declined because of the legal processes, but instead sent a detailed written response.
(Govan VO) Medihelp says: It is “deeply conscious” and aware the case involves a child and a family. It wishes all patients could receive every possible treatment. It argues funding cases like Zachary’s could jeopardise the pooled contributions of its 190 000 members.
(Govan link) Medihelp is one of the oldest medical aids, apparently showing up for 120 years... I think Zach’s family would disagree.
(Michenay) I don't think they care. I think that they made a decision right at the beginning to go up against us. they are just following through on that decision regardless of what it costs them.
(Govan VO) The CMS case hasn’t been finalized, because both Medihelp and the family are appealing that decision.
In the meantime, Megan’s legal team went back to court to enforce Judge Millar’s 2022 order for Medihelp to pay. After years of various court processes, the latest ruling in November was scathing of Medihelp’s conduct.
(Jacques reads) “The applicant has deliberately chosen not to abide by the order…”

Unique Selling Point: Zachary’s Law: STORY PITCH A David vs Goliath story of when a Medical Aid Defies the Law ONE LINE SUMMARY: A mother won in court. Twice. But her medical aid still refuses to pay for her child’s rare disease. Now, a judge has said: obey — or go to jail to the medical aid. It started as one mother’s desperate fight to save her son. Now, it could change how medical aids treat every South African patient. A 5-year-old boy, Zachary De Wet, has Hunter Syndrome (MPS II) — a rare genetic condition that slowly attacks the body and the brain. There’s only one treatment that can slow it down: Elaprase, an enzyme-replacement drug. Yet, his family’s medical aid — Medihelp — refused to pay. Initially, Medihelp argued in court that Elaprase was not a Prescribed Minimum Benefit (PMB). But in 2022, a judge rejected that argument — ruling that not only is the condition a PMB, but that the standard for determining treatment is simple: “What does the state do?” And in this case, the state provides Elaprase. They then argued that while the state gives the drug, it’s only done through a “compassionate programme” — so they weren’t obliged to fund it. That single interpretation has now exploded into one of the biggest legal fights in South African healthcare. THE STORY: Zachary’s mother, Michaney De Wet, turned to attorney Megan Harrington-Johnson — a name Carte Blanche audiences will recognise. We previously told Megan’s own story, when she fought for her daughter’s future after a childhood cancer diagnosis — using cutting-edge science to preserve her little girl’s chance of having children one day. Now, she’s on the other side of the table — fighting for another family, against a medical aid giant. Her firm took the case pro bono in 2021, arguing that because the state provides Elaprase, it must also be covered by private medical aids under the law governing PMBs. Different layers: The First Win (2022) Judge Millar rules in favour of the De Wets: • Hunter Syndrome (MPS II) is a PMB condition. • Elaprase is the standard public-sector treatment — so Medihelp must pay for it. • The ruling sets a powerful precedent for rare-disease coverage. Despite this, Medihelp refused to pay, and backed by an army of advocates representing other medical schemes, they appealed. According to Kelly du Plessis of Rare Diseases South Africa, this fight went far beyond a single family’s struggle. “This wasn’t just one fund defending itself — it was the entire medical-aid industry protecting its profit model.” Layer 2: The Showdown (2025) Last week, Judge Swanepoel handed down a scathing judgment. He upheld the earlier decision and went further — finding Medihelp in contempt of court for ignoring Judge Millar’s order. He wrote that Medihelp’s conduct was “cynical, aggressive, and mala fide” — and warned that if they don’t pay, the Principal Officer could be imprisoned. It’s one of the most blistering rebukes of a medical aid ever seen in South Africa. Megan HJ: Two judges. Two rulings. One medical aid defying them both. CHARACTERS: • Zachary (5) — bright, funny, and brave. He still receives his life-saving treatment through donations, but his future depends on this ruling being enforced. • Michaney De Wet — a mother who’s spent years fighting bureaucracy while trying to keep her son alive. • Megan Harrington-Johnson — lawyer, mother, and rare-disease advocate. Her personal story gives this case an extraordinary emotional echo. • Rare Diseases South Africa (Kelly du Plessis) — the NGO that’s stepped in where medical aids have failed, supporting families like Zachary’s across the country. EXTRA INFORMATION: Carte Blanche first explored this issue in 2022 — exposing how families with rare diseases were being denied essential, life-sustaining treatments. This case takes that story a decisive step further. At its core, it asks a fundamental question of South African healthcare law: must medical aids meet the same standard of care provided by the state? Since that earlier report, medical aids have continued to delay or deny enzyme replacement therapies (ERTs) — even when medical and legal evidence shows these treatments must be fully funded. Now, for the first time, a medical aid has been found in contempt of court for refusing to provide care-related treatment. The ruling sets a powerful new precedent: PMB conditions can’t be defined by whether the state pays for treatment, but by whether that treatment is available within the state system — even if supplied through a compassionate or donor programme. We’ll, of course, request an interview with Medihelp — though it’s unlikely they’ll agree. In that case, we can head to their head offices in Brooklyn, Pretoria, and give viewers some context about who they are. Medihelp has been operating since 1905 and today serves more than 200,000 members. In 2023, the scheme reported R2.39 billion in assets and paid out R3.3 billion in claims. As Principal Officer, Varsha Vala is the public face of Medihelp’s leadership — and in this story, she’s the person whose accountability will come under scrutiny if the scheme continues to defy two court orders. I believe this story will hold strong until January, as Medihelp is expected to seek leave to appeal to the Constitutional Court. That means the legal battle — and public interest — will remain active. Even if the court process takes time, the core issue of accountability won’t date: a major medical aid defying two High Court orders and facing possible contempt proceedings is a story that will stay relevant and develop further in the months ahead. Based in Pretoria, Medihelp is one of the largest non-profit medical aid schemes - with 190,000 members. The de Wets decided to take the Goliath to court. (Recap over) (Govan link) Today, three years later, they stand at the centre of a legal showdown involving High Court judgments, the medical regulator, and the possibility of a medical-aid executive going to jail. (Jacques) Before we went to the High Court, I remember I just spent about half an hour grieving his death, and he was still there. (Govan) Oh no! (Jacques) I had to come to terms with the fact that, soon, he might not be with us. (Govan VO) The family is represented pro bono by a Fourways-based legal team led by attorney Megan Harrington-Johnson. (Megan) My heart went out to them, being in the situation where you have a critically ill child, and you are now worrying about having to pay for their treatment. (Govan VO) This complex case has played out in two arenas: the courts, and the medical-aid regulator - the CMS or Council for Medical Schemes. (graphic timeline) In August 2022, High Court Judge Anthony Millar ruled in the family’s favour. (Megan) What Judge Millar found was that pending the outcome of the dispute in the CMS, so the Council for Medical Schemes, all treatments and associated costs for Zachary's condition, which he confirmed is a PMB condition, must be paid for. (Govan VO) Medihelp later sought leave to appeal this ruling, but meanwhile began to pay for Elaprase. Zach responded well. (Michenay) So within about three or four months, we very clearly had that shift from him being sick every six weeks to not having that at all. (Govan VO) Millar’s order only applied until the CMS process was complete. The family’s complaint about Medihelp’s refusal to pay was heard in December 2022. (Megan) There is a dispute as to what the standard of care he should be receiving is, because whilst he has to have all of his treatment paid for, it's defined in very broad terms in the Medical Schemes Act. So, it says that he should have medical management paid for, and there's a dispute as to what constitutes medical management. (Govan VO) Medihelp argues that it’s not obliged to pay for Elaprase - only for broader medical management like hospitalisation. The CMS initially agreed. (Megan) They said that Judge Miller's order fell away. Unfortunately, the medical aid stopped paying for his treatment. (Govan VO) Medihelp reasoned that Millar’s order was meant to secure immediate access to Elaprase when Zach had none – and once it was donated, the basis for that order fell away. (Jacques) That was a shock, because we'd just gone into the rhythm of how life was supposed to be. And now his life saving drug is ripped away from you. (pause) (Megan) So a third party funder has stepped in to donate the Elaprase to him until such time as the CMS complaint is finalised. (Govan VO) After appealing the initial CMS finding, the family won the appeal in June 2025: The ruling said Elaprase should be funded. But with a caveat for Medihelp. (Megan) So the last decision of the CMS strangely found that whilst Zachary's condition should be a PMB entitlement, they were excused from paying because their solvency ratio fell below the threshold of 25%. (Govan VO) In other words, Medihelp didn't have enough money in its fund to pay for this treatment - at least according to the CMS. (Govan) But isn't the solvency ratio meant to protect the members, not the medical aides? (Megan) Yes, correct. (Govan link) We asked medihelp for an on-camera interview but they declined because of the legal processes, but instead sent a detailed written response. (Govan VO) Medihelp says: It is “deeply conscious” and aware the case involves a child and a family. It wishes all patients could receive every possible treatment. It argues funding cases like Zachary’s could jeopardise the pooled contributions of its 190 000 members. (Govan link) Medihelp is one of the oldest medical aids, apparently showing up for 120 years... I think Zach’s family would disagree. (Michenay) I don't think they care. I think that they made a decision right at the beginning to go up against us. they are just following through on that decision regardless of what it costs them. (Govan VO) The CMS case hasn’t been finalized, because both Medihelp and the family are appealing that decision. In the meantime, Megan’s legal team went back to court to enforce Judge Millar’s 2022 order for Medihelp to pay. After years of various court processes, the latest ruling in November was scathing of Medihelp’s conduct. (Jacques reads) “The applicant has deliberately chosen not to abide by the order…” (Jacques reads): “The applicant’s explanation for not paying… does not hold water… it is untenable and should be rejected.” (Megan) They are compelled to pay for everything right now in terms of judgement as ordered from 2022. (Govan VO) The judge warned that disobeying a court order — known as contempt of court — could have personal consequences for Medihelp’s principal officer - Varsha Vala - including arrest in her capacity as representative of the medical aid. (Megan) We've never had a case where a medical aid has been found to be in contempt of a court order. This is the first time in South African legal history that that has happened. (Govan VO) Medihelp says it accepts it was found in contempt. But it says because it has asked for leave to appeal the latest court order, that order is suspended until the appeal process is finalised. (Jacques) Part of the argument from Medihelp's side was that we are getting treatment donated for Zach. And so why should they be obligated to pay for it. (Govan VO) The court rejected Medihelp's argument for not paying for Elaprase while the CMS process is ongoing. (Jacques) They created the situation that someone else had to step in, that feels like they are just playing a game with the life of your son. And wherever they can find a gap not to meet their obligations, they'll take it. (Govan VO) Medihelp says it's not deliberately defying the courts and maintains that it will comply with whatever final decision is made by the CMS Appeal Board or higher courts. (Govan) So you expect them to keep fighting after this? (Jacques) Absolutely. We expect them to take it as far as they possibly can. (Govan VO) PMBs are based on treatments available in public healthcare. Elaprase is available in some state hospitals, but only through donor funding as their budgets are limited. And because Zach is already on medical aid, he can’t access those programmes. So the question before the CMS final appeal board remains: does Medihelp have to cover what is AVAILABLE in a state hospital, or what the state will PAY for? Medihelp argues that treatment needs to be funded by the state to meet the standard for PMB. (Govan VO) This legal back-and-forth has taken its toll on the entire family — Zachary isn’t their only child; he also has a sister, Emma. (Jacques) I’ll never forget the day when Emma came to me, and she looked me in the eye, and she said, ‘Daddy, I don’t want Zach to die’…for her to have a brother for the next 10 to 20 years. (Govan) Oh man! (Michenay) Emma cried. She understands that something's going on and she understands that we have to keep winning in order for her brother to just keep getting his medication. (Govan link) In the end, all the numbers, and legal arguments fade — and what remains is one child’s life. Because how this case ends won’t just affect Zachary — it will shape how medical aid funds everyone. (Govan VO) If Zach's case succeeds at the CMS, it will be historic. (Megan) It will set the precedent for what the PMB standard of care is for Zachary's rare condition. And that will, of course, then probably be binding on many medical aid schemes in the country. (Govan) This could benefit other children in the future, probably children who haven't even been born yet. (Megan) Yes it would. (Govan VO) Doctors say Zachary’s disease is stable on the medication — giving him what every sick child deserves: more time. metadata.Unique Selling Point: Zachary’s Law: STORY PITCH A David vs Goliath story of when a Medical Aid Defies the Law ONE LINE SUMMARY: A mother won in court. Twice. But her medical aid still refuses to pay for her child’s rare disease. Now, a judge has said: obey — or go to jail to the medical aid. It started as one mother’s desperate fight to save her son. Now, it could change how medical aids treat every South African patient. A 5-year-old boy, Zachary De Wet, has Hunter Syndrome (MPS II) — a rare genetic condition that slowly attacks the body and the brain. There’s only one treatment that can slow it down: Elaprase, an enzyme-replacement drug. Yet, his family’s medical aid — Medihelp — refused to pay. Initially, Medihelp argued in court that Elaprase was not a Prescribed Minimum Benefit (PMB). But in 2022, a judge rejected that argument — ruling that not only is the condition a PMB, but that the standard for determining treatment is simple: “What does the state do?” And in this case, the state provides Elaprase. They then argued that while the state gives the drug, it’s only done through a “compassionate programme” — so they weren’t obliged to fund it. That single interpretation has now exploded into one of the biggest legal fights in South African healthcare. THE STORY: Zachary’s mother, Michaney De Wet, turned to attorney Megan Harrington-Johnson — a name Carte Blanche audiences will recognise. We previously told Megan’s own story, when she fought for her daughter’s future after a childhood cancer diagnosis — using cutting-edge science to preserve her little girl’s chance of having children one day. Now, she’s on the other side of the table — fighting for another family, against a medical aid giant. Her firm took the case pro bono in 2021, arguing that because the state provides Elaprase, it must also be covered by private medical aids under the law governing PMBs. Different layers: The First Win (2022) Judge Millar rules in favour of the De Wets: • Hunter Syndrome (MPS II) is a PMB condition. • Elaprase is the standard public-sector treatment — so Medihelp must pay for it. • The ruling sets a powerful precedent for rare-disease coverage. Despite this, Medihelp refused to pay, and backed by an army of advocates representing other medical schemes, they appealed. According to Kelly du Plessis of Rare Diseases South Africa, this fight went far beyond a single family’s struggle. “This wasn’t just one fund defending itself — it was the entire medical-aid industry protecting its profit model.” Layer 2: The Showdown (2025) Last week, Judge Swanepoel handed down a scathing judgment. He upheld the earlier decision and went further — finding Medihelp in contempt of court for ignoring Judge Millar’s order. He wrote that Medihelp’s conduct was “cynical, aggressive, and mala fide” — and warned that if they don’t pay, the Principal Officer could be imprisoned. It’s one of the most blistering rebukes of a medical aid ever seen in South Africa. Megan HJ: Two judges. Two rulings. One medical aid defying them both. CHARACTERS: • Zachary (5) — bright, funny, and brave. He still receives his life-saving treatment through donations, but his future depends on this ruling being enforced. • Michaney De Wet — a mother who’s spent years fighting bureaucracy while trying to keep her son alive. • Megan Harrington-Johnson — lawyer, mother, and rare-disease advocate. Her personal story gives this case an extraordinary emotional echo. • Rare Diseases South Africa (Kelly du Plessis) — the NGO that’s stepped in where medical aids have failed, supporting families like Zachary’s across the country. EXTRA INFORMATION: Carte Blanche first explored this issue in 2022 — exposing how families with rare diseases were being denied essential, life-sustaining treatments. This case takes that story a decisive step further. At its core, it asks a fundamental question of South African healthcare law: must medical aids meet the same standard of care provided by the state? Since that earlier report, medical aids have continued to delay or deny enzyme replacement therapies (ERTs) — even when medical and legal evidence shows these treatments must be fully funded. Now, for the first time, a medical aid has been found in contempt of court for refusing to provide care-related treatment. The ruling sets a powerful new precedent: PMB conditions can’t be defined by whether the state pays for treatment, but by whether that treatment is available within the state system — even if supplied through a compassionate or donor programme. We’ll, of course, request an interview with Medihelp — though it’s unlikely they’ll agree. In that case, we can head to their head offices in Brooklyn, Pretoria, and give viewers some context about who they are. Medihelp has been operating since 1905 and today serves more than 200,000 members. In 2023, the scheme reported R2.39 billion in assets and paid out R3.3 billion in claims. As Principal Officer, Varsha Vala is the public face of Medihelp’s leadership — and in this story, she’s the person whose accountability will come under scrutiny if the scheme continues to defy two court orders. I believe this story will hold strong until January, as Medihelp is expected to seek leave to appeal to the Constitutional Court. That means the legal battle — and public interest — will remain active. Even if the court process takes time, the core issue of accountability won’t date: a major medical aid defying two High Court orders and facing possible contempt proceedings is a story that will stay relevant and develop further in the months ahead. (Govan Link) To understand this case, we need to talk about something called a Prescribed Minimum Benefit — or a PMB. It’s the law that protects every medical-aid member in South Africa. And for families like Zachary’s, it can be the difference between life and death. (Govan VO) PMBs are the treatments that medical aids must pay for — in full — no matter which plan you’re on, or how much the treatment costs. The law says the standard of care is what the state provides. So if a government hospital offers a particular treatment for a PMB condition, every medical aid has to match it. Link: In Zachary’s case, the state treats Hunter Syndrome with a drug called Elaprase. That means Elaprase is the legal minimum standard of care. Michaney: “When he learns something new, you’re almost… holding your breath. Jacques: “If his heart deteriorates… if he loses his ability to walk or talk… there’s nothing we can do. Megan Harrington-Johnson and her firm’s team took the case on pro bono, Medihelp was ordered to pay within 30 days. (MEGAN HJ) That judgment was clear — the law says medical aids must fund PMB conditions in full. But Medihelp chose to fight instead of pay. The billing codes were wrong — basically, ‘computer says no.’ You’d think the battle ended there right? VO: But this decision was again appealed by both sides. Megan: They said that despite it being a PMB, Medihelp didn’t have to pay because weren’t solvent. The law looks at whether the treatment is available in the public sector, not who pays for it. And in Zachary’s case, the state does use Elaprase. Which means medically and legally, it is PMB care.
